clue.text: This implant ultimately mimics bone

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the last letters of these two words
to ape someone is to mimic them

explanation.surface: A surgeon's implant made to imitate a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is medical, and apt: a stapes prosthesis really is implanted in the ear. 'Ultimately' works on both 'This' and 'implant'.
explanation.definitionFit: The stapes is the tiny stirrup-shaped bone of the middle ear, the smallest in the human body.

clue.text: Swimmer finally leaving for Portugal, gets plane

indicators.note: the final letter departs from the fish

parts.note: a turbot is a fish, so a swimmer
pro means for, in favour of
P is the international vehicle code for Portugal

explanation.surface: A fish loses its way before heading off to Portugal, where it catches a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' looks like a link word before Portugal, but it means in favour of and supplies its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A turboprop is an aircraft driven by a propeller turned by a gas turbine.

clue.text: They might do the conveyancing for your last move

definitions.text: They might do the conveyancing for your last move

parts.words: They might do the conveyancing for your last move
parts.note: surface reading: solicitors handling the legal paperwork when you move house for the final time; setter's reading: physically conveying you, in a coffin, on your final journey to the grave

explanation.walkthrough: Conveyancing is the British legal work of transferring property when you move house; here it is taken literally as carrying, and the last move is your funeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Pall-bearers are the people who carry or escort a coffin at a funeral service.

clue.text: Fashion label

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion label' reads as one noun phrase, a designer brand; it is two separate definitions, and both can be verbs.
explanation.definitionFit: To style something is to call it by a particular name, and style also means a prevailing mode of dress.

clue.text: Meet the cost of smooth, hard pavement

parts.note: to foot the bill is to pay it
to pat down is to smooth
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Paying to have a pavement laid smooth and hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth, hard' looks like a pair of adjectives describing the pavement; both are wordplay, and smooth is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the pavement is the raised walkway beside a road, which is also called a footpath.

clue.text: Conclusion drawn from income gap

indicators.note: something drawn from a phrase is pulled out of it intact

parts.note: sitting across the two words

explanation.surface: An economist's conclusion about the income gap.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from the end of 'income' into 'gap'.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, hence the end or final part of anything.

clue.text: Topic this writer raised in article

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something turns it upside down

parts.note: the setter referring to themself

explanation.surface: A writer brings up a topic in an article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' in the surface is a piece of journalism; in the wordplay it is the grammatical article THE.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the subject or main idea of a talk, essay or piece of writing.

clue.text: Wall in Bosnia's prime locations provide defence?

indicators.note: only the letters at prime-numbered positions are kept, so every letter in a non-prime slot is taken away

explanation.surface: A wall in Bosnia sits at strategic spots offering protection.
explanation.walkthrough: Number the letters of WALLINBOSNIA: those in positions 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, the prime numbers, are A, L, I, B, I. 'prime locations' looks like real estate but means prime-numbered positions.
explanation.definitionFit: To alibi someone, used as a verb, is to vouch that they were elsewhere, a defence against an accusation.

clue.text: Supply teacher's area

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, meaning flexibly, so the letters bend into a new shape

parts.note: the fodder, used whole

explanation.surface: A supply teacher's patch of the school.
explanation.walkthrough: A supply teacher is a British substitute teacher; here 'supply' is an adverb, supple-ly, and the 's means is.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectare is a metric unit of land measurement equal to ten thousand square metres.

clue.text: Wind breaks through form of weather protection

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it

parts.note: by means through, as in by way of
to wind something is to roll it up

explanation.surface: A gale breaking through a weatherproof shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Wind here is the verb that rhymes with find, not the weather. BROLLY is British slang for an umbrella.
explanation.definitionFit: A brolly is an informal British name for an umbrella, which shields you from rain.

clue.text: Church pastor peeled a cold vegetable

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: peeling strips the outer skin, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: a cleric is a clergyman, such as a pastor

explanation.surface: A church minister peels a chilly vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peeled' strips the skin from the pastor word, just as you would peel the vegetable itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Celeriac is a variety of celery grown for its swollen edible root, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Lively German ladies sob over musicians essentially releasing new patriotic song from Berlin

indicators.note: lively means active and bouncing about, so the letters are rearranged
releasing means the abbreviation for new is let go from German
essentially takes the essence, the centre letter, of musicians

explanation.surface: Animated German women weep over the band in a scene that seems set in Berlin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Berlin' looks like the German capital; it is Irving Berlin, who wrote the song.
explanation.definitionFit: Irving Berlin wrote God Bless America, a patriotic American anthem first sung by Kate Smith in 1938.

clue.text: Ray Harryhausen made you stab skeletons from Olympia, conclusively with animation

indicators.note: animation brings still things to life, so the letters move
conclusively points to the conclusion, so each word gives its final letter

parts.words: Harryhausen made you stab skeletons from Olympia
parts.note: the final letter of each of the seven words

explanation.surface: Ray Harryhausen animating sword-fighting skeletons in a film set in ancient Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray looks like part of the name Ray Harryhausen, the stop-motion animator famous for the skeleton fight in Jason and the Argonauts; it is the definition, standing alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunbeam is a single ray or shaft of sunlight, so the first name doubles as a synonym.

clue.text: West maybe carrying bridge team — one might be 22

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within

parts.note: Mae West, the Hollywood actress, as one example of a Mae
North and South form a partnership in bridge

explanation.surface: A bridge player sitting West partnering a team, with a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: West looks like the bridge seat, fitting 'bridge team'; it is Mae West. 22 is HOUSING MINISTER, read as a house for a minister.
explanation.definitionFit: A manse is the house provided for a Presbyterian or other Nonconformist minister, so it is literally housing a minister.

clue.text: People massaging tense American politician get unquestioning approval

parts.note: people who rub, as masseurs do
grammar abbreviation
standard abbreviation
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Masseurs loosening up a tense American politician to win approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Tense reads as a stressed adjective describing the politician; it is the grammar term, giving T.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber stamp is automatic sanction given without scrutiny, like a stamp pressed onto every document.

clue.text: Address atmosphere during theatre around rehearsal

indicators.note: turned around means facing the other way
something happening during something else sits within its span

parts.note: the National Theatre in London, wrapped around what follows
a web address
the air around us

explanation.surface: Talking about the mood backstage at a theatre during a rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: Address is a web address, not a speech, and theatre is the National Theatre, London's state-funded playhouse. The whole string turns back to front at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial run is a practice test before the real performance or launch, exactly what a rehearsal is.

clue.text: Loveless 23 with King starting quarrel

indicators.note: the king's letter comes at the start

parts.note: R is short for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: love is zero, the letter O, so it is dropped

parts.note: the answer to clue 23 is union

explanation.surface: A loveless marriage, with a monarch thrown in, begins a row.
explanation.walkthrough: UNION, the answer to 23, loses its O (love, a zero score in tennis) to give UNIN, with R at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: A run-in is an argument or confrontation, as in a run-in with the police.

clue.text: Attractive priest with cake on the counter

indicators.note: counter means against or opposite, so the order runs the opposite way

parts.note: Eli, the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible
a bun is a small cake

explanation.surface: A handsome priest with a cake laid out on a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: The counter looks like a bakery counter where the cake would sit; it means contrary, so the pair is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nubile describes a young woman considered sexually attractive, so it serves as a synonym here.

clue.text: Modern coffee right on time

parts.note: a milky espresso drink
standard abbreviation
a day is a time or period, as in 'in my day'

explanation.surface: A coffee chain boasting modern service that arrives right on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' just places the second piece after the first in this across-style charade, even though this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Latter-day means belonging to recent times, a contemporary version of an older figure or thing.

clue.text: Pre-noon power nap's mostly controlling bad temper

indicators.note: pre means before, so the shortened nap word goes before the noon letter
most of the word, so its final letter is lost
controlling means holding in check, so the outer pieces hold the power letter

parts.note: a nap is a short sleep
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A short, energising sleep before midday keeps an ill mood in check.
explanation.walkthrough: SLEEP minus its last letter gives SLEE, before N; that SLEEN holds P after its S.
explanation.definitionFit: Spleen means anger or ill humour, from the old belief that the organ was the seat of bad temper.

clue.text: Contrived solution discovered after school

indicators.note: the solution piece comes after the school piece
dis-covered means with its covering removed, so the outer letters go

parts.note: a remedy is a solution to a problem

explanation.surface: An answer was found after school had finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' reads as found but means dis-covered, with its covering of outer letters taken off.
explanation.definitionFit: To scheme is to plot or devise, so a plan that was schemed was contrived.

clue.text: They cycled around in France and Spain with energy — they're sometimes capped

indicators.note: the cycled word goes around the other letters
the letters go round in a cycle, the front ones moving to the end

parts.note: taken as written, before its letters move
et is French for and
E is the international vehicle code for Spain
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Some people cycled around France and Spain with gusto, perhaps wearing caps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They cycled' looks like people on bikes, but the word itself is cycled. The definition is fair because dentists fit caps on teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeteeth are the canine teeth of the upper jaw, and a dentist may crown them.

clue.text: Once government position ruins something — I will be needing correction

indicators.note: a spelling that needs correcting is wrong as it stands, so its order must change

parts.note: the fodder, three words

explanation.surface: A former minister admits he wrecked something and needs to put it right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' belongs to the definition: the Housing Minister post has at times sat in the British cabinet and at other times not.
explanation.definitionFit: The Housing Minister is a British ministerial role overseeing homes and planning policy within government.

clue.text: Club working to support college

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting something means sitting beneath it

parts.note: short for university
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A club getting to work backing a college.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the supporting piece goes underneath, so it comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: A union is an association of members, like a students' union, which is a social club.

clue.text: Perhaps gusset isn't replaced to cover embarrassment initially

indicators.note: the rearranged letters cover the initial letter, putting it inside
the letters are put back in a new order
picks the first letter of embarrassment

explanation.surface: A gusset that isn't put back hides a blush.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of ISN'T are rearranged as INST, which goes around E, the first letter of 'embarrassment'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gusset is a piece of fabric set into a garment, so it is one example of an insertion.

clue.text: Stuck-up men inspired by Harry's complaint

indicators.note: in a down clue, stuck up means pushed upwards, so it reads bottom to top
breathed in, so one piece is drawn inside another

parts.note: to harry is to pester, or nag
other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Snooty men inspired by a man called Harry, who complains.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry looks like a name; it is the verb meaning to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: A groan is a deep sound of pain or displeasure, and so an expression of grievance.

clue.text: Gall bladder's close to bottom? Not at all!

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom is the end, so the letter is moved there

parts.note: gall and nerve both mean cheek or audacity

indicators.note: the close of something is its end, so only its final letter counts

parts.note: its final letter, which already sits in the middle of the word above

explanation.surface: A medical question about whether the gall bladder lies near the bottom, flatly denied.
explanation.walkthrough: Gall bladder is one phrase in the surface; Gall is the wordplay and 'bladder's close' is the R, which is shifted from the middle of the word to the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Never means at no time, an emphatic refusal, just as 'Not at all!' is an exclamation of denial.

clue.text: Powerful men called first for promotion

indicators.note: first means placed at the front of the answer
something called out is spoken, so it is heard rather than seen

parts.note: males are men; said out, it is the plural of post
hot as in strong or potent

explanation.surface: Strong men being called up first to be promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: Powerful men suggests hotshots, but the pieces swap order: the men come first.
explanation.definitionFit: A mailshot is advertising material posted to many potential customers at once, a form of marketing.

clue.text: Six workers wanting hot food

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the hot letter is missing

parts.note: hands are manual workers
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Half a dozen labourers want hot meals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' looks like desiring but means lacking: HANDS loses H.
explanation.definitionFit: Viands is an old-fashioned word for items of food, provisions.

clue.text: Meaning daughter for example is eating out

parts.note: standard abbreviation

indicators.note: eating something takes it inside

parts.note: e.g., exempli gratia
not in, as when someone is away from home

explanation.surface: A daughter who is, for instance, eating out at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eating out' is one phrase for dining at a restaurant; eating is the container and out is the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Denoting means signifying or indicating, so it works as the present participle of 'mean'.

clue.text: Refunds from agent, when handling unknown

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative

indicators.note: to handle something is to hold it in your hands

parts.note: as in 'as I arrived'
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: Getting refunds from an agent who is handling something unknown.
explanation.walkthrough: Unknown is the algebra letter Y, held inside the word for when.
explanation.definitionFit: To repay is to give money back to someone, which is what a business does when it refunds.
